report.source_text: A male patient in his 40s presented with a 1 week history of periocular swelling, redness and decreased vision in his right eye. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 24 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. Both pupils responded normally to light, indicating no relative afferent pupillary defect. On slit-lamp examination, the right eye showed ciliary congestion, anterior chamber cells 4+ and vitreous cells 2+. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed fibrous proliferation superior and temporal to the hyperaemic oedematous disc with peripapillary exudation superior and inferior to the disc and peripapillary haemorrhage, accompanied by macular edema that was confirmed by optical coherence tomography (OCT) (figure 1). The left eye examination was normal. A presumptive diagnosis of panuveitis in the right eye was made, and the patient was initially treated with topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics and IOP-lowering medication, pending laboratory results.

report.source_text: Laboratory tests for infections, including HIV, Rapid Plasma Reagin, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination antibody and QuantiFERON-TB Gold, were negative. Serological testing for toxoplasmosis was positive for IgG, and the complete blood count revealed elevated eosinophils at 8%, with an absolute eosinophil count of 6.16 x 108 cells/L (normal <5 x 108 cells/L). An immunofluorescent assay (IFA) for IgM and IgG anti-Bartonella henselae showed no evidence of B. henselae-specific antibodies. A brain CT scan showed no intraocular parasites, and oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy exhibited normal findings.

report.source_text: Following surgery, the patient received postoperative management consisting of topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 2 hours, atropine 1% two times per day and oral prednisolone at a dosage of 1 mg/kg/day, with tapering doses. By postoperative day 7, the anterior chamber reaction had subsided and become quiet, with slight improvement observed in vitreous cells. Consequently, albendazole at a dosage of 400 mg two times per day was initiated for a 21-day course.

report.source_text: Three weeks post-surgery, a significant improvement was noted in the vitreous reaction. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a whitish scar in the superior and temporal regions of the optic disc, accompanied by a persistent macular star (figure 5). At 6 weeks postoperation, the macula status remained similar to that observed at the third week postoperation, with a reduction in the hard exudates (figure 6). BCVA in the right eye had improved to 6/9, indicating a successful outcome in managing the intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A male patient in his 40s presented with a 1-week history of periocular swelling, redness, and decreased vision in his right eye, diagnosed presumptively as panuveitis. Initial treatment with topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics, and IOP-lowering medication was started. One week later, a live nematode was observed in the anterior chamber of the right eye. Following surgical removal, the nematode was identified as G. spinigerum by the Department of Microbiology. Laboratory tests ruled out several other infectious causes, though toxoplasmosis IgG was positive and eosinophils were elevated. Postoperatively, the patient received topical and oral corticosteroids, atropine, and a 21-day course of albendazole. By postoperative day 7, the anterior chamber reaction had subsided, and vitreous cells improved. Three weeks post-surgery, significant improvement in vitreous reaction was noted, and at 6 weeks, BCVA improved to 6/9, with reduced hard exudates, indicating a successful outcome.
